title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
author: Immanuel Kant
translator: Varies by edition (e.g., Mary Gregor, H. J. Paton, Thomas Kingsmill Abbott)
publication_date_analyzed: varies (often most recent standard English translation)
edition_analyzed: Common modern academic translation (e.g., Cambridge University Press, Mary Gregor, 1997)
target_audience: Researchers in ethics and moral theory
University students in humanities and social sciences
General readers interested in classic philosophy
core_themes: The autonomy of the will and moral law
The concept of duty and the categorical imperative
The distinction between hypothetical and categorical imperatives
The relationship between reason and morality
primary_purpose: To identify and explicate the fundamental principles of moral philosophy—specifically, to establish a 'metaphysics of morals' independently of empirical knowledge and to articulate the concept of the categorical imperative as the supreme principle of morality.

structure_format.narrative_style: Systematic, argumentative, and rigorous exposition typical of Enlightenment philosophy, with abstract reasoning and structured logical development.
structure_format.organization: Divided into a preface and three main sections (often called 'propositions' or 'chapters'), each building on the previous to develop the groundwork for moral law.
features: Occasional references to contemporary moral thought

key_concepts_lessons: Morality is rooted in reason, not inclination.
The highest good is to act out of respect for the moral law.
Only actions performed out of duty, in accordance with universalizable maxims, have genuine moral worth.
The categorical imperative—'Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law'—is the central criterion for moral action.
Humans must always be treated as ends in themselves, never merely as means.
Moral principles must be universal and necessary, not contingent or based on desires.
notable_features: Introduction of the categorical imperative as a moral test
Influential division between 'empirical' and 'a priori' knowledge
Canonical text for modern moral philosophy
cultural_historical_context: Written in late 18th-century Prussia, during the Enlightenment, as part of Kant's larger critical philosophy project. The work responds to contemporary debates about the foundations of morality and aims to provide a rational, universally valid principle independent of tradition or religious doctrine.
reception_impact: Seminal influence on modern ethics, establishing Kant as a central figure in Western philosophy
Formed the basis for deontological (duty-based) moral theories
Widely studied, debated, and critiqued in both academic and applied ethics
Challenged by utilitarian and virtue-ethics traditions, but still core reading in ethical philosophy
comparable_titles: Critique of Practical Reason by Immanuel Kant
The Elements of the Philosophy of Right by G. W. F. Hegel
